lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 1.

items.signText: Dear all, your writing test is next Wednesday. You will not be allowed to use dictionaries, but you can bring your own pens and a watch. Please check the noticeboard on Monday to find out which room you are in. Ms Okafor
items.question: What does Ms Okafor tell the students?
options: a) The writing test will take place on Monday.
b) The test room will be announced on Monday.
c) They should bring a dictionary to the test.
items.explanation: She asks students to "check the noticeboard on Monday to find out which room you are in". The test itself is "next Wednesday", and dictionaries are not allowed: "You will not be allowed to use dictionaries".

items.signText: Laptops can be borrowed for use in this room only. Show your student card at the desk. All laptops must be returned 15 minutes before the centre closes.
items.question: What does the notice say about the laptops?
options: a) Students may only use them inside the centre.
b) Students can take them home if they show their card.
c) Students can keep them for 15 minutes at a time.
items.explanation: Laptops are "for use in this room only", so they cannot leave the centre. The student card is shown "at the desk" to borrow one, not to take it home, and the 15 minutes refers to returning laptops "before the centre closes", not to how long you can use one.

items.signText: To all students: tickets for Friday’s trip to Bath are now on sale at reception. Payment is by card only. The coach leaves at 8.15 sharp and won’t wait for anyone who is late. Anna, Student Office
items.question: What should students who want to go on the trip do?
options: a) Pay the coach driver on Friday morning.
b) Arrive at 8.15 to get their ticket.
c) Buy a ticket at reception using a card.
items.explanation: Tickets are "on sale at reception" and "Payment is by card only". Nobody pays on the coach, and 8.15 is the time the coach "leaves", so it is too late to buy a ticket then.

items.signText: Intermediate Group B: this week’s classes will be in Room 4 on the ground floor while new heating is put in here. Your teacher and lesson times stay the same.
items.question: What does the notice say?
options: a) Group B’s lessons will start at a different time.
b) Group B will study in a different room this week.
c) Group B will have a new teacher for this week.
items.explanation: The notice says "this week’s classes will be in Room 4" instead of Room 12. It also says "Your teacher and lesson times stay the same", so neither the teacher nor the time changes.

items.signText: Marta – sorry, I can’t make our conversation exchange at 4 today! My dentist has moved my appointment. Could we do tomorrow at the same time instead? Same place, the library café. Let me know. Kenji
items.question: What does Kenji want to do?
options: a) Have the exchange on a different day
b) Stop doing the conversation exchange
c) Meet somewhere other than the library café
items.explanation: Kenji asks "Could we do tomorrow at the same time instead?", so he wants to move the exchange to another day. He says "Same place, the library café", and he only cancels today’s meeting, not the whole exchange.

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 3.
lesenParts.textTitle: On her toes: an interview with Isla Mackenzie
lesenParts.text:
Isla Mackenzie is seventeen and comes from Glasgow, and last month she won a place at a famous dance school in London. We asked her about her life so far.

When did you start dancing?
I started when I was six. My older sister went to ballet classes, and I had to wait for her every Saturday until her class finished. I watched through the window and copied all the steps that the older girls did. One day the teacher noticed me and invited me in. My sister stopped after a year, but I never did.

Was ballet always your favourite?
No, it wasn’t at first. To be honest, I found it quite boring as a child because there were so many rules. Then, when I was eleven, I tried contemporary dance, which felt much freer. Suddenly I understood the point of ballet. It gives you strength and control. Now I do both styles.

How much do you train?
About twenty hours a week. I go to school as normal, and then I dance every evening and on Saturdays as well. My friends often go to the cinema while I’m training. That used to upset me, but now I accept it. I see them on Sundays, and they come to all my shows.

Have you ever wanted to give up?
Only once, when I was fourteen. I hurt my ankle badly and couldn’t dance for four months. I felt completely lost because dancing was my whole life. My physiotherapist gave me exercises that I did every day. During that time I started to watch other dancers more carefully. I noticed small details in their movements. Strangely, I came back a better dancer.

How did the audition for the London school go when you finally went there?
I was terribly nervous because there were three hundred people for only thirty places. First we did a ballet class, and then we each performed a short piece. I chose a contemporary piece by my own teacher. In the middle I slipped slightly, but I didn’t stop. I just carried on and smiled. Afterwards one of the judges told me that she liked that moment the most. In her opinion, it showed my character.

What are you worried about?
Moving away from home, mostly, because I’ve never lived alone, and I can’t cook at all! My mum is giving me lessons this summer so that I don’t starve. London is expensive too, so money is a bit of a worry. Luckily, I’ve got a grant that pays for the fees.

What would you say to young people who want to dance?
Dance because you love it, not for fame. Most dancers never become stars, and that’s fine. The joy is in the dancing itself.

questions.question: How did Isla begin going to ballet classes?
questions.explanation: Isla watched "through the window" and then "the teacher noticed me and invited me in." Her sister was already in the class, but Isla never asked to join; the teacher invited her.
options: a) Her school offered free lessons on Saturdays.
b) A teacher saw her outside the class.
c) Her mother booked lessons for her sixth birthday.
d) She asked her sister if she could join her class.

questions.question: What does Isla say about ballet?
questions.explanation: After trying contemporary dance, "Suddenly I understood the point of ballet. It gives you strength and control." She did not always like it ("I found it quite boring as a child"), and she did not stop: "Now I do both styles."
options: a) She has always liked it more than other styles.
b) She stopped doing it when she found contemporary dance.
c) She still finds all its rules boring.
d) Contemporary dance showed her why it was useful.

questions.question: How does Isla feel now about missing evenings with her friends?
questions.explanation: Isla says: "That used to upset me, but now I accept it." She was upset in the past, not now, and her friends "come to all my shows", so she is not worried about losing them.
options: a) She has learned to accept the situation.
b) She worries that they will stop being her friends.
c) She is still upset when they go out without her.
d) She wants to train less so she can join them.

questions.question: What does Isla say about her ankle injury?
questions.explanation: During the injury she "started to watch other dancers more carefully" and "noticed small details in their movements." She could not dance "for four months", not a year, and she started contemporary dance at eleven, before the injury.
options: a) It still hurts when she does some movements.
b) It was the reason she tried contemporary dance.
c) It made her study other dancers carefully.
d) It kept her away from dancing for a whole year.

questions.question: Why did one of the judges like Isla’s audition?
questions.explanation: Isla slipped but "just carried on and smiled", and the judge "liked that moment the most" because "it showed my character." So the performance was not perfect, and the piece was "by my own teacher", not a famous dancer.
options: a) She performed her piece without a single mistake.
b) She was able to dance in two different styles.
c) She carried on calmly after she slipped.
d) She chose a piece by a well-known dancer.

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 4.
lesenParts.textTitle: From the sofa to the finish line
lesenParts.text:
Two years ago, Owen Price could not run for a bus. The 45-year-old taxi driver from Cardiff spent most of his day sitting down, and he hardly ever did any exercise. (1) ________ His doctor told him that his blood pressure was too high and that he needed to become more active.

Owen decided to start with something small. He downloaded a free app that mixed one minute of running with ninety seconds of walking. (2) ________ After nine weeks, however, he could run for thirty minutes without stopping, and he felt prouder than he had felt for years.

That was when his daughter, Carys, suggested a marathon. Owen laughed at first. (3) ________ However, Carys had already found a six-month training plan for beginners. It started with three short runs a week and slowly added longer runs at weekends.

The plan was not always easy to follow. In January, the weather was terrible and Owen caught a bad cold. (4) ________ Instead of giving up, he went back to shorter runs for a fortnight until he felt strong again.

On race day, the crowds along the streets were enormous. Owen remembered the advice from Carys and started slowly. (5) ________ He finished in five hours and twelve minutes, and Carys was waiting at the finish line with a cup of tea. Now he wants to run the race again next year and beat his own time.

questions.question: Read the text "From the sofa to the finish line". Which sentence (A–H) best fits gap 1?
questions.explanation: The text moves from his old life ("hardly ever did any exercise") to "His doctor told him"; a "check-up at his local surgery" is where this happened, and "Everything changed" marks the turning point. The sentence about running ten kilometres the next morning cannot fit, because Owen "could not run for a bus".
options: A) Carys agreed to run the whole race next to him.
B) Everything changed after a routine check-up at his local surgery.
C) For ten days he could not run at all, and he began to worry that he had lost all his fitness.
D) Luckily, the sunny weather made his long weekend runs a pleasure.
E) At first, even this was hard, and he often had to stop and rest.
F) Because of this, he still had energy for the last and most difficult part of the race.
G) The next morning, he ran ten kilometres without stopping.
H) He had never run further than five kilometres, and a marathon is more than forty-two.

questions.question: Read the text "From the sofa to the finish line". Which sentence (A–H) best fits gap 2?
questions.explanation: "even this" refers to the gentle mix of "one minute of running with ninety seconds of walking", and "At first" contrasts with "After nine weeks, however". The sentence about running ten kilometres the next morning is wrong, because after nine weeks he could only run "for thirty minutes", and he started with "something small".
options: A) Carys agreed to run the whole race next to him.
B) Everything changed after a routine check-up at his local surgery.
C) For ten days he could not run at all, and he began to worry that he had lost all his fitness.
D) Luckily, the sunny weather made his long weekend runs a pleasure.
E) At first, even this was hard, and he often had to stop and rest.
F) Because of this, he still had energy for the last and most difficult part of the race.
G) The next morning, he ran ten kilometres without stopping.
H) He had never run further than five kilometres, and a marathon is more than forty-two.

questions.question: Read the text "From the sofa to the finish line". Which sentence (A–H) best fits gap 3?
questions.explanation: This sentence explains why "Owen laughed at first": he had never run far, and a marathon is very long. "However" in the next sentence then introduces the answer to this problem, the "training plan for beginners". The sentence saying Carys agreed to run next to him is wrong, because at the end she "was waiting at the finish line".
options: A) Carys agreed to run the whole race next to him.
B) Everything changed after a routine check-up at his local surgery.
C) For ten days he could not run at all, and he began to worry that he had lost all his fitness.
D) Luckily, the sunny weather made his long weekend runs a pleasure.
E) At first, even this was hard, and he often had to stop and rest.
F) Because of this, he still had energy for the last and most difficult part of the race.
G) The next morning, he ran ten kilometres without stopping.
H) He had never run further than five kilometres, and a marathon is more than forty-two.

questions.question: Read the text "From the sofa to the finish line". Which sentence (A–H) best fits gap 4?
questions.explanation: After "caught a bad cold", this sentence describes the result: he "could not run at all" and was worried. This leads to "Instead of giving up". The sentence about sunny weather contradicts "the weather was terrible".
options: A) Carys agreed to run the whole race next to him.
B) Everything changed after a routine check-up at his local surgery.
C) For ten days he could not run at all, and he began to worry that he had lost all his fitness.
D) Luckily, the sunny weather made his long weekend runs a pleasure.
E) At first, even this was hard, and he often had to stop and rest.
F) Because of this, he still had energy for the last and most difficult part of the race.
G) The next morning, he ran ten kilometres without stopping.
H) He had never run further than five kilometres, and a marathon is more than forty-two.

questions.question: Read the text "From the sofa to the finish line". Which sentence (A–H) best fits gap 5?
questions.explanation: "Because of this" refers to "started slowly": by not running too fast at the beginning, he still had energy at the end, and then "He finished". The sentence saying Carys ran the race next to him is wrong, because she "was waiting at the finish line".
options: A) Carys agreed to run the whole race next to him.
B) Everything changed after a routine check-up at his local surgery.
C) For ten days he could not run at all, and he began to worry that he had lost all his fitness.
D) Luckily, the sunny weather made his long weekend runs a pleasure.
E) At first, even this was hard, and he often had to stop and rest.
F) Because of this, he still had energy for the last and most difficult part of the race.
G) The next morning, he ran ten kilometres without stopping.
H) He had never run further than five kilometres, and a marathon is more than forty-two.

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 5.
lesenParts.text: The summer I turned sixteen, I got my first job, in a small bookshop in the town centre. I saw a notice in the window and (1) ______ for it that same afternoon. The owner, Mrs Hughes, (2) ______ me a few questions about myself and then told me I could start the (3) ______ Saturday. I was delighted, but also a bit worried because I had never worked before. On my first day I had to (4) ______ a green shirt with the name of the shop on it, and I spent the morning learning how to (5) ______ the till. It was much more complicated than it looked! During the first week I (6) ______ lots of mistakes. Once I gave a customer change for twenty pounds when she had paid with a ten, and another time I put all the cookery books in the travel section. Mrs Hughes was always patient, though, and the other staff helped me whenever the shop got busy. Earning my own money made me feel much more independent, and I am going back next summer.

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (1).
questions.explanation: You apply for a job: "I saw a notice in the window and applied for it". Offered for, signed for (receive a parcel) and filled for do not mean asking to be given a job.
options: a) applied
b) offered
c) signed
d) filled

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (2).
questions.explanation: The collocation is ask a question: "Mrs Hughes asked me a few questions about myself". We do not say made, did or said questions to someone.
options: a) did
b) asked
c) said
d) made

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (3).
questions.explanation: The writer was told "I could start the following Saturday", meaning the next one. The last or previous Saturday is in the past, so the writer cannot start then, and the early Saturday has no meaning.
options: a) previous
b) early
c) last
d) following

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (4).
questions.explanation: You wear clothes: "I had to wear a green shirt". Dress needs a person as object (dress a child), put needs on (put on a shirt) and try also needs on (try on a shirt).
options: a) put
b) try
c) wear
d) dress

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (5).
questions.explanation: The writer spent the morning "learning how to use the till", the machine for taking money. Do and make the till are not possible, and hold the till does not mean operating it.
options: a) hold
b) use
c) do
d) make

questions.question: Choose the word that best fits gap (6).
questions.explanation: The collocation is make a mistake: "I made lots of mistakes", followed by two examples. Did, got and had mistakes are not correct English.
options: a) made
b) had
c) did
d) got

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 6.
lesenParts.text: Four years ago, my English teacher organised an online exchange with a school in Edinburgh. Every student in our class was given a partner to write to, and mine was a girl (1) ______ name was Isla. At first I was not very keen (2) ______ the idea, because I have never enjoyed writing long messages. But the emails from Isla were so funny that I always replied straight away. Soon we were chatting by video every weekend, (3) ______ though we had never met. Last July my parents finally agreed to take me to Scotland. On the train I felt nervous, and (4) ______ worried me most was that we would have nothing to say to each other face to face. In fact, (5) ______ was no reason to worry at all. Isla was waiting on the platform holding a big sign with my name on it, and we started talking at once. I stayed with her family for a week and even had a little room of my (6) ______ at the top of the house. Now we are planning her visit to my town next spring.

questions.question: Write ONE word that fits gap (1).
questions.explanation: Whose is the possessive relative pronoun: "a girl whose name was Isla" means a girl, and her name was Isla. Who or that cannot be followed directly by a noun like name.

questions.question: Write ONE word that fits gap (2).
questions.explanation: The fixed phrase is keen on something: "I was not very keen on the idea". No other preposition is used after keen with a noun.

questions.question: Write ONE word that fits gap (3).
questions.explanation: Even though introduces a surprising contrast: they chatted every weekend "even though we had never met". Only even fits before though in one word here.

questions.question: Write ONE word that fits gap (4).
questions.explanation: What means the thing that and starts the subject of the clause: "and what worried me most was that we would have nothing to say". No other single word can start this clause.

questions.question: Write ONE word that fits gap (5).
questions.explanation: There was introduces something that exists (or here, does not exist): "there was no reason to worry at all". It was no reason is not correct English.

questions.question: Write ONE word that fits gap (6).
questions.explanation: The fixed pattern is a + noun + of + my own: "had a little room of my own", meaning a room only for the writer. No other word fits after of my.

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 1.
horenParts.transcript:
Man: So which animal are you going to photograph for the competition?
Woman: Everyone will take pictures of the lions, so I don’t want to do that. I thought about the penguins, but they’re inside, behind glass, and you get terrible reflections.
Man: What about the giraffes? They’re outside, and the light’s lovely there in the afternoon.
Woman: Yes, they’re the ones. I’ll go over there after lunch.

Man: You’re back early from your walk.
Woman: It started raining. But guess what I saw by the river? A deer! It was just standing there, drinking.
Man: Really? I’ve only ever seen foxes round here.
Woman: I usually see rabbits in the field next to the river, but there weren’t any today. The deer ran off as soon as it heard me.

Woman: Well, I’ve checked Max all over. He’s healthy, but he’s a bit heavy for a dog of his size.
Man: Oh dear. Should I change his food, or give him less?
Woman: No, his food is fine, and he’s eating the right amount. The problem is exercise. How long are his walks?
Man: About fifteen minutes, twice a day.
Woman: That isn’t enough for a young dog like Max. Try to make each walk at least forty minutes, and bring him back to see me in a month.

Man: I’ve started volunteering at the animal centre on Saturdays.
Woman: Really? What do you do there? Clean the cages?
Man: Most volunteers do that, but they’ve got enough people for it now. Last week I fed the rabbits, but this Saturday they’ve asked me to take some of the dogs out for walks.
Woman: That sounds like the best job of all.

Woman: Welcome to Hill Farm, boys and girls. Now, I know you all want to ride the ponies, but they’re having a rest at the moment, so we’ll do that at two o’clock. The baby lambs are asleep in the barn, so we’ll visit them after the ponies. So let’s start by giving the goats some food. Take a bag each from the box by the gate, and follow me.

Woman: Have you seen Tiger? I’ve looked under the bed and in all the cupboards.
Man: He was on the garage roof earlier, sitting in the sun.
Woman: He isn’t there now. I’ve just looked.
Man: Wait, listen. Can you hear that? It’s coming from inside the garage. I left the door open when I got the bikes out. He must have gone in there.
Woman: Oh yes, there he is, next to the bikes. Silly cat!

Woman: Did you hear? Our dog Bella had her puppies last night.
Man: Oh, that’s exciting! How many?
Woman: The vet thought there would be eight, but in the end there were five.
Man: Are you going to keep them all?
Woman: No way! Six people have already asked us for one, so finding homes for them won’t be a problem.

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 2.
horenParts.transcript:
Man: Have you been to the new café where the bookshop used to be?
Woman: Yes, I went on Saturday. I was sad when the bookshop closed, I must admit. But the café’s lovely. They’ve kept some of the old shelves, and there are books you can borrow while you have your coffee.
Man: Isn’t it expensive, though?
Woman: A bit more than the place by the station, but I don’t mind. It feels like the bookshop never really left.

Woman: Are you going to the meeting at the library tonight?
Man: Yes. I expect most people will complain about parking.
Woman: It’s the building work that bothers me. It’s so noisy.
Man: That’ll be finished in a month. No, I’m going because they want to turn the empty land behind the school into a playground, and some people are against it. My kids have got nowhere to play round here, so I want to speak up for it.
Woman: Good for you.

Woman: Did you read in the local paper that the council wants to close Mill Road to cars on Sunday mornings?
Man: I did. The idea is that children can play in the street.
Woman: I’m not sure many children would use it, actually. And the shopkeepers are worried they’ll lose customers.
Man: I think they’ll get more people walking past. But the council should ask the people who live here before it decides anything.
Woman: Absolutely. Nobody’s asked us a thing.

Woman: Did you see in the paper that the Regal Cinema is going to be turned into flats?
Man: Yes. It’s sad. I saw my first film there.
Woman: Lots of people are saying the council should repair it and open it again.
Man: I’d love that, but who would go? It’s been closed for eight years, and everyone watches films at the big cinema by the shopping centre now. Young people round here can’t find anywhere to live, so flats make sense.
Woman: I suppose you’re right.

Man: How was the street party in the end?
Woman: Well, it was hard work. Weeks of letters, phone calls, borrowing tables. I nearly gave up twice.
Man: Was it expensive?
Woman: No, the council lent us the tables for free, so it hardly cost anything. And on the day about sixty people came. I talked to neighbours I’d never spoken to in ten years of living there.
Man: So will you do it again next year?
Woman: Definitely. I’m really glad I did it.

Man: How’s the new flat in Ashford Street?
Woman: I love it. I was worried because it’s near the main road, but my bedroom’s at the back, so I hardly hear the traffic.
Man: And the neighbours?
Woman: That’s the best thing. The day I moved in, the woman next door brought me a cake, and the man upstairs helped me carry my sofa. In my old street nobody even said hello.
Man: Is it far from work?
Woman: Twenty minutes on the bus. About the same as before.

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 3.
horenParts.transcript:
Man: And now some exciting news for all you young writers out there. Here at Radio Harbourside we’re running our Young Writers’ Competition again, and this year it’s bigger than ever.

First of all, who can enter? Last year the competition was open to anyone between eleven and eighteen, but we had so many entries from older teenagers that this year we’re making it just for younger writers. So, if you’re aged between eleven and sixteen, you can take part.

Now, the subject. Last year’s stories were all about friendship, and we read some wonderful ones. This year we want you to write a story about a journey. It could be a trip to the other side of the world or just the walk to school. Use your imagination!

Your story mustn’t be longer than eight hundred words. I know some competitions ask for five hundred, but we want to give you a bit more space. Please don’t go over the limit, though, or the judges won’t read it.

Here’s the really exciting part. The three best stories will be read out on the radio in June. Not by me, I’m pleased to say, but by a well-known actor. We can’t tell you who yet, but you’ll certainly recognise the voice.

And the prizes? Everyone on the shortlist gets a set of books, and the winner will receive a laptop, which we hope will help with all your future writing.

To enter, just send your story to the address on our website before the thirtieth of April. Don’t forget to put your name and age at the top. We won’t be sending emails to tell people the results. Instead, the winners will be contacted by phone in the middle of May, so make sure you include a phone number for a parent or carer.

Good luck, everybody. We can’t wait to read your stories.

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 4.
horenParts.transcript:
Interviewer: My guest today is Aisha Bello, who’s just twenty-three and runs her own recycling business in Leeds. Aisha, tell us what you do.

Aisha: We collect old jeans from charity shops, from people’s wardrobes, from anywhere really, and turn them into bags, cushions and pencil cases. Last year we saved about four tonnes of denim from going to the rubbish tip.

Interviewer: How did the idea start?

Aisha: At university I shared a flat with three other students, and when we moved out, the amount of clothing we threw away shocked me. I’d always thought of myself as someone who cared about the environment, and suddenly I felt quite ashamed. That’s really what got me started. Making money didn’t come into it at first.

Interviewer: Was it difficult to get going?

Aisha: The sewing wasn’t a problem. My grandmother taught me when I was small. The hard part was persuading shops to stock our products. Some of them said recycled things looked cheap. I had to keep going back with better and better samples, and eventually one shop in York said yes.

Interviewer: You now have six people working for you. What’s that like?

Aisha: I love it, although being a boss was a big change. At first I tried to check everything myself, and I was exhausted. Now I trust the team to make their own decisions, and honestly, they often have better ideas than I do.

Interviewer: Your bags aren’t cheap, are they?

Aisha: No, and I won’t pretend they are. Every one is made by hand here in Leeds, and we pay our staff properly. Some customers do complain, but most of them understand that if you want something made fairly, it’s going to cost a bit more.

Interviewer: Some people say small recycling businesses can’t really make a difference. What do you think?

Aisha: I understand why they say it. One small company won’t save the planet. But I think we do something important by showing people that old things can be beautiful. When customers see what we make, they start looking at their own clothes differently, and that matters more than the tonnes we collect.

Interviewer: And what’s next for you?

Aisha: People keep telling me to open a big factory, but I’m not interested in growing too fast. I’d rather stay small and do things properly. What I would like is to run workshops in schools, so that children can learn to repair their own clothes.

Interviewer: Aisha Bello, thanks for talking to us.

b) She saw a chance to make a lot of money.

questions.explanation: "The hard part was persuading shops to stock our products." Sewing was easy for her: "The sewing wasn’t a problem. My grandmother taught me".

c) Getting shops to sell what she made

c) She would rather go back to working alone.

options: a) Sell her products in other countries
b) Teach children to mend clothes
c) Open a large factory near Leeds

schreibenParts.task:
Read this email from your English-speaking friend Tom and the notes you have made.

From: Tom
Subject: Our cooking evening

Hi!
I’m really looking forward to the cooking evening we’re organising for our class next Friday. [Note 1: Me too!] About twelve people are coming. Should we cook one big meal together or ask everyone to bring a dish? [Note 2: Say which and why] I can bring plates and glasses from my house. What else do we need? [Note 3: Tell Tom] Also, my cousin Ellie is staying with us that weekend. Is it all right if she comes too? [Note 4: Yes, because …]

Cheers,
Tom

Write your email to Tom using all the notes. Write about 100 words.

Choose ONE of these questions. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Question 2 – Article
You see this announcement on an English-language website for teenagers.

Articles wanted!
MY FAVOURITE MEAL
What is your favourite meal? Who makes it, and when do you usually eat it? Why do you like it so much?
Write an article answering these questions. The best articles will appear on our website next month.

Write your article.

Question 3 – Story
Your English teacher has asked you to write a story.
Your story must begin with this sentence:
Suddenly there was smoke everywhere in the kitchen.

Write your story.

sprechenParts.title: Part 1 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Part 1 – Interview
The examiner asks you some questions about yourself. Answer each question and give some extra information.

Do you like spending time outdoors? Why or why not?
Where do you go when you want to be in nature?
What did you do the last time you went to the countryside or the beach?
Which season do you like best? Why?
Would you like to go camping? Why or why not?

sprechenParts.title: Part 2 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Part 2 – Photo description
Look at the photograph. It shows four young people collecting rubbish on a sandy beach. They are all wearing gloves, and two of them are holding large black bags. One of them is picking up a plastic bottle from the sand. Next to them there are some more bags full of rubbish. Behind them you can see the sea and some rocks, and the sky is blue. Tell us what you can see in the photograph.

Talk for about one minute.

sprechenParts.title: Part 3 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Part 3 – Collaborative task
A school wants to do more to help the environment. Here are some ideas the students are thinking about.

recycling bins in every classroom
a vegetable garden in the school grounds
a week when everyone walks or cycles to school
turning off lights and computers at lunchtime
a sale of second-hand uniforms and books
solar panels on the school roof

Talk together about how each idea could help the environment. Then decide which idea the school should try first.

Talk together for about two or three minutes.

sprechenParts.title: Part 4 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Part 4 – General conversation
The examiner asks you and your partner some questions about recycling and protecting nature. Give your opinion and talk to your partner too.

What do you and your family recycle at home?
Do you think people throw away too many things? Why?
What can young people do to protect nature?
Is it better to buy new things or second-hand things? Why?
Have you ever taken part in an activity to help the environment?
